You want to know what the nested number means and how far to trust it.
This page runs no code. It says why a tuned model's own score cannot be
trusted, which quantity the nested number describes, and how to read its
standard error. It also covers fold disagreement and when nesting is worth
its cost. The worked example is `vignette("nested-cv")`.

## The case for nesting

Most people tune with cross-validation, keep the best setting, and score
it once on a held-out test set. That test score is one number from one
split of the data. Nothing in it says whether the split is representative.
Nested cross-validation scores the same tune-and-fit steps on several
outer splits instead. It reports the mean across those splits and how far
the score moves from one split to the next. Each outer split also tunes on
its own, so no outer score is the score of a winner picked for scoring
well.

When you tune with cross-validation, you try several settings, the
candidates, and keep the one with the best score. Scores are noisy, and the
best of several noisy numbers tends to look better than it is. So the
winner's score overstates what the model will do on new data, by an amount
nothing in the output reveals.

At a small sample size the noise is large, so the winner's score can come
out no better than an honest one. Distrust it for how it was chosen,
high or low.

The procedure is every step you run on the data: resample, tune, pick a
setting, fit. Each outer fold runs it from scratch on its own analysis
rows and scores the fitted setting once on assessment rows the tuning
never saw.

The number `collect_metrics()` reports is the number to report for the
model you deploy. It describes the whole tune-and-fit procedure, measured
on rows the procedure never saw. The deployed model is that same procedure
run once more on all the data. So the estimate is its number, and there is
no second one to compute for it.

## The quantity estimated

The number `collect_metrics()` reports is the procedure's error when it
runs on each fold's training rows and is scored on fresh data. Bayle et
al. (2026) call that the k-fold test error of the procedure.

The estimate has a scope. No score is computed on the deployed model
itself, because everything the data can say went into building it. The
estimate is not a verdict on the parameter values that one run chose. It
does not say what a larger or a different training set gives, because the
procedure ran on this one alone. And it is the error on this data, not
that error averaged over every training set the same source can produce. That average
describes the method rather than this data. Luo and Barber (2026) prove
that any assumption-free test of that method-level quantity needs a
dataset many times larger than the training set. So this package offers
no such test.

## A slight pessimism

The number tends to look a little worse than the procedure deserves. Every
outer fold trains on its analysis rows only, so every model scored is built
on less data than the model you finally deploy. Less data usually means
worse predictions. Varma and Simon (2006) separate this training-size
effect, which can go either way, from the selection effect, which is always
optimistic.

Varma and Simon (2006) ran nested cross-validation on null data with 40
samples, where the true error is 50.0%, and got 54.2%. They attribute the
4.2-point overshoot to training on 39 rows rather than 40. Wilimitis and
Walsh (2023) compared methods on 41,121 hospital visits against a held-out
benchmark. Nested cross-validation was among the most pessimistic, by
roughly 1 to 2% of AUROC and 5 to 9% of AUPR. The same study reports one
cell where the nested estimate came out optimistic instead.

The gap is a property of the estimator, not a prediction about any one run.
It is no license to adjust the reported figure upward.

## The standard error

`std_err` is the standard error of the mean across the outer folds. It is
the standard deviation of the fold scores divided by the square root of
their number. It is not the fold-to-fold spread, which is larger by that
factor. `collect_metrics(res, summarize = FALSE)` gives the per-fold scores.
It is not a confidence interval, and this package ships no inference on
the nested estimate.

## Comparing two workflows

Suppose you run the loop on two workflows and one comes back lower. Nothing
in the output says whether the difference is real, because there is no
valid interval to subtract. Bayle et al. (2026) give a sharper reason. A
cross-validation interval for one procedure is valid when that procedure is
stable. Stable means that changing one training row shifts its errors by
little, compared with how spread out those errors are. Two procedures can
each be stable while their difference is not, and the difference is what
the interval has to cover. That difference is least stable when the
two procedures are similar. A gap between two nested estimates is a reason to
look closer, never a result.

The same holds for a set of workflows run through one design with
`nested_workflow_map()`. Choosing the best estimate is itself a selection
that no outer loop scored, so the package offers no ranking or
best-workflow function for the set.

## Disagreement between folds

When the folds split over a parameter, the data does not pick its value
clearly. The estimate is fine, because it already averages over this
variability. What suffers is any story about the selected parameters being
the right ones.

As two candidates' predictions converge, which one wins a given fold
becomes close to a coin flip (Bayle et al., 2026).

## The cost of nesting

Whether nesting pays depends on how much room the selection step had to
overfit. Tibshirani and Tibshirani (2009) measured that room on pure noise,
where the true error rate is 0.5. With 400 observations and 100 features,
the tuned score was under 3 points too good. With 40 observations and 1000
features, the best tuned score of nearest shrunken centroids read 0.384,
which is 11.6 points below the true 0.5. Even there the learner mattered:
an SVM was 2.5 points too good and a tree only 0.2. In short, the bias is largest with wide data, a big
grid, and a preprocessing step the loop has to redo. That paper's remedy is
a correction, not nesting.

Nesting removes little when the data is tall and the search is small. Wilimitis
and Walsh (2023) ran that case, 41,121 visits and a modest grid. Nesting
bought nothing but the pessimism above, at a cost that grew quadratically in
the fold count. Their advice, and this package's: nest when there are many
features for the sample size and the search is wide, if you can afford the
compute.

Small data is not safe without nesting. Vabalas et al. (2019) simulated
pure noise, where the honest accuracy is 50%. Cross-validation without
nesting still reported better than chance at a sample size of 1000. Nested
cross-validation stayed at chance at 96.5% of the sample sizes they tried,
almost all of them. The bias thins with sample size and does not disappear.

## Feature selection inside the workflow

If your pipeline selects features, put that step in the recipe inside the
workflow you pass in. The loop here re-estimates the whole workflow inside
every fold. Anything done to the data before the call is not re-estimated.
No result here can tell that it happened. Vabalas et al. (2019) compared two
mistakes: leaving feature selection outside the loop, and leaving parameter
tuning outside it. The first was far more damaging.

comparison with cross-validation. *arXiv:2508.04409*.
